summary: Describes subprograms at the University of California, Santa Barbara that let PL/I programs on the IBM 360/75 use the ARPANET. Like its Fortran counterpart in RFC 119, it provides an interface to the local Network Control Program, with a completion code variable tracking each socket that is not closed.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 120 describes assembly-language subprograms that let PL/I programs at UCSB use the ARPANET through the local NCP. The subprograms manage sockets and report operation results through completion codes.

subtitle: An assembly-language interface for UCSB PL/I programs to use the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: UCSB PL/I programs needed a callable interface to the Network Control Program and its socket operations.
tldr.mechanism: Assembly-language subprograms provide operations to open, close, send, receive, and inspect sockets, with completion-code variables reporting outcomes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 120 documents a library implemented for PL/I programs compiled at UCSB on its IBM 360/75 system.

today: RFC 120 documents a PL/I subprogram library implemented at UCSB for its IBM 360/75. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: A PL/I Interface to the NCP
sections.content:
The subprograms described in RFC 120 were implemented at UCSB for PL/I programs running on the IBM 360/75. They provide an assembly-language interface between user programs and the local Network Control Program (NCP).

Each socket that is not closed has a unique completion-code variable. It identifies the local socket and contains a code when an operation completes. The RFC specifies that these variables use the PL/I attribute BINARY FIXED(31,0)ALIGNED.
sections.plainLanguage: A PL/I program can call subprograms that ask the NCP to manage network sockets. Each active socket has a variable that identifies it and records operation results.

sections.title: Opening and Closing Sockets
sections.content:
OPEN supports CONNECT, LISTEN, and ACCEPT. CONNECT requests a connection to a foreign socket; LISTEN waits for a call to a local socket; ACCEPT completes a connection after a successful LISTEN. The requested operation must match the socket's state.

CLOSE returns a socket to the closed state. It refuses a pending LISTEN, aborts a CONNECT, or allows data in transit on an established connection to reach the foreign socket before closing.
sections.plainLanguage: OPEN can request a connection, wait for one, or accept one. CLOSE ends the socket and handles any connection attempt or data still in progress.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving, and Checking
sections.content:
WRITE sends a specified number of bits from a buffer, and READ receives bits into a buffer. Both accept a time limit measured in tenths of a second. If the limit expires, completion code 252 indicates that the operation started but remains incomplete.

CHECK immediately reports a socket's status, foreign socket, and send/receive deficit. ID finds the socket associated with a completion-code variable, and SIGNAL sends a user-defined signal to the foreign process.
sections.plainLanguage: WRITE sends data and READ receives it. CHECK reports the socket's state, while ID and SIGNAL provide additional socket operations.

sections.title: On-Line System Messages
sections.content:
For the On-Line System operators, messages contain a one-byte operation code, a two-byte length in bits, and text. Code 0 is NOP, code 1 carries EBCDIC characters for display, code 2 carries keys for immediate execution, and code 3 carries keys to execute after all data for the receive operation arrives.

A string of messages ends with a NOP header called a trailer. The RFC also describes operators for writing to and reading from the On-Line System console.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message header tells the On-Line System what the following text contains and how to use it. A NOP header marks the end of the message string.
